And one who doesn't walk quite the way the rest of you do. You... drift. Like a song somebody's humming.
I walk. I have feet.
So you do, sweetling. So you do.
And the one in front walks like someone leaving. Come here, Wren Halloway.
How do you know my—
Ysolde's girl. I knew your grandmother's step, and your mother's. You have both. Your mother hated being told that.
...She still does.
Good. Now. What has Cassian sent me?
Wren opens the case. Tamsin's fingers find a fork without searching, the way you find the latch of your own door in the dark.
She strikes it once against her cane and holds it to her ear. The note is pure and thin, and it goes on much longer than it should.
Tamsin's smile goes away.
...It sings a note I almost know.
Is something wrong with it?
Like a word in a language I used to speak. Like a name I heard in a dream and lost on waking.
I've listened to the Dawnsong every morning for fifty-one years, child. I know every note of it the way you know your mother's voice. This is one of them. And it is not.
The Hierophant had them made in the Cathedral. To harmonize the Lanterns, against the Gloam—
I know what he said. Cassian always says exactly the right thing.
I've known him since he was a boy who couldn't sleep unless a lamp was burning. I trust him to be exactly who he is.
That is what worries me.
She lays the fork back in its velvet, gently, like something that might bite.
Take it to Halvard at Frosthollow, north in the Greyspine. He has forgotten more about the Dawnsong than the Choir ever knew. If Halvard says it is true, I will set it in my light with my own hands.
And if he says it isn't?
Then you will have learned something about the world, Wren Halloway. That's what sixteen is for.
Pip has wandered up the dais steps, very casually, toward the little silver bell on Tamsin's belt.
Tamsin's hand closes on his wrist without looking.
And you, little cat.
I was just — admiring. Professionally.
Twelve in the spring!
Eleven and a _HALF_.
You're the only one of them without a light on you. I can feel it. Like a cold spot in a warm bath.
Yeah, well. Choir says sixteen. Rules is rules. Not that I care. Crests are for people with houses.
_(quietly)_ Is that what they told you?
...Nobody had to tell me.
The world's getting darker, little cat. I can't see much. But I can see that.
I'd like you to have something to hold on to.
Keeper — you can't. Kindling a child is forbidden. There are laws—
Five years in an Aurenne cell, I believe. Are you going to tell on me, Mender?
...I'm going to write it down somewhere and not tell anyone where.
Is it... safe? For him?
Nothing worth doing is safe, squire. You of all people know that.
Well, Pipkin Tallow? Will you step into my light?
How do you know my— nobody calls me—
Pip stands in the Lantern's light. His fists are clenched. His chin is up. He looks very small.
The light goes all the way through him, warm as fresh bread — and for the first time anyone can remember, Pip forgets to look for the exits.
ROGUE?! The light called me a _THIEF?!_
...I mean. Fair.
Pip's Crest awakens — *Rogue*! His Crest Arts can now be used in battle.
Wren. _Wren!_ I got one! I got a Crest! Nobody from the gutters ever— not before sixteen, not _ever_, some of 'em—
Make way! Rogue Pipkin Tallow, first of his name!
Put me DOWN, you big— okay, don't put me down yet.
Welcome to the trade, kid. Rule one: never tell anyone your real age.
Way ahead of you.
Pip has a light now. It is small. It is very loud.
Tamsin laughs — a real laugh, surprised out of her.
They usually are, the small ones.
Go on, all of you. The caravans for the Greyspine leave from the north yard. Ask for Oyelaran, and tell him I said he owes me.
And Wren Halloway — you walk like someone leaving. Make sure you know what you're walking toward.
